'''''Ulmus davidiana''''', also known as the '''David elm''', or '''Father David elm''' (named after the botanist [[Armand David]], who collected specimens), is a small [[deciduous]] tree widely distributed across China, Mongolia, Korea, Siberia, and Japan, where it is found in wetlands along streams at elevations of 2000–2300 m (6,500–7,500 ft).<ref name=Fu>Fu, L., Xin, Y. & Whittemore, A. (2002). Ulmaceae, in Wu, Z. & Raven, P. (eds) ''Flora of China'', Vol. 5 (Ulmaceae through Basellaceae). Science Press, Beijing, and Missouri Botanical Garden Press, St. Louis, USA. [http://flora.huh.harvard.edu/china/PDF/PDF05/Ulmus.pdf]</ref> The tree was first described in 1873 from the hills north of [[Beijing]], China.<ref name=Heybroek>{{cite journal | last = Heybroek | first=Hans M.|journal = Proceedings of the Dutch Elm Disease Symposium and Workshop, October 5–9, Winnipeg, Manitoba|title = The Japanese elm species and their value for the Dutch elm breeding program|pages = 78–90|date=1981|url=http://krishikosh.egranth.ac.in/bitstream/1/2055474/1/MPKV-1936.pdf}}</ref>

The tree suffered confusion with ''[[Ulmus uyematsui]]'', a Taiwanese species widely planted in China, at the Morton Arboretum. 
 
==Classification==
Two varieties of ''Ulmus davidiana'' are recognized: [[Ulmus davidiana var. davidiana|var. ''davidiana'']], occurring only in China, and [[Ulmus davidiana var. japonica|var. ''japonica'']] <small>Rehder</small>, the more widely ranging Japanese Elm.<ref name=Fu/> Some authorities, however, do not consider ''japonica'' to be a variety of ''U. davidiana'', ''The Illustrated Flora of the Primorsky Territory, Russian Far East'' (2019), for example, maintaining ''U. japonica'' as a species.<ref>Kozhevnikov, Andrey E.; Kozhevnikova Zoya V.; Kwak, Myounghai; Lee, Byoung Yoon (2019), ''Illustrated Flora of the Primorsky Territory (Russian Far East)'', National Institute of Biological Resources, Incheon, South Korea</ref><ref>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:837143-1 ''Ulmus japonica'' (Rehder) Sarg., Plants of the World Online]</ref> In 1916 [[Arnold Arboretum]] described the two as different species.<ref>[https://archive.org/details/mobot31753003014922/page/261/mode/2up ''U. davidiana'' <small>Planch.</small> (no. 13) and ''Ulmus japonica'' <small>Sarg.</small> (no. 12), in Charles Sprague Sargent, ed., ''Plantae Wilsonianae: an enumeration of the woody plants collected in western China for the Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University during the years 1907, 1908, and 1910 by E. H. Wilson'', Vol.3, p.258-262 (Cambridge, Mass., 1916)]</ref> [[Harold Hillier]] originally (1973) listed and described ''japonica'' as a variety of ''U. davidiana'',<ref>''Hilliers'' Manual of Trees & Shrubs. Ed. 3, 399, (1973); David & Charles, Newton Abbot, UK</ref> but [[Hillier Nurseries|Hillier]]'s separated the two as distinct species in later editions of their ''Manual of Trees and Shrubs''.<ref>''Hilliers' Manual of Trees & Shrubs''. Ed. 6, 369, 370, (2002); David & Charles, Newton Abbot, UK</ref>

==Description==
''Ulmus davidiana'' is considered to have a remarkable resemblance to the [[Ulmus americana|American elm (''U. americana'')]] in all but ultimate size.<ref name=Ware>Ware, G. (1995). Little-known elms from China: landscape tree possibilities. ''Journal of Arboriculture'', (Nov. 1995). International Society of Arboriculture, Champaign, Illinois, US. [http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/fletcher/programs/nursery/metria/metria8/m87.pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071130221822/http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/fletcher/programs/nursery/metria/metria8/m87.pdf |date=2007-11-30 }}</ref> The tree grows to a maximum height of 15 m (50 ft), with a relatively slender trunk < 0.3 m (1 ft) [[d.b.h.]] supporting a dense canopy casting a heavy shade. Its bark remains smooth for a comparatively long time, before becoming longitudinally fissured. The leaves are [[leaf shape|obovate]] to obovate-elliptic < 10 cm (4 in) × < 5 cm (2 in), with a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] of about 10 mm, according to the protologue (the original description);<ref>''Ulmus davidiana'' Planchon, in Candolle, Prodr. 17: 158. 1873</ref> the ''Flora of China'' description gives a petiole range of 5-10 mm with an extreme of 17 mm,<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200006324 ''U. davidiana'' description, Flora of China, vol.5 p.7, efloras.org]</ref> while [[Alfred Rehder|Rehder]] described the petiole simply as 'short'; <ref>''Ulmus davidiana'' Planchon, in Rehder, ''Manual of Cultivated Trees and Shrubs'' p.187. 1934, New York, MacMillan.</ref>  the upper surface is rough.<ref>{{Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris (France) |id=P00721891 }} Sheet labelled ''Ulmus davidiana''; Armand David type specimen (1), fruit and new leaves; eastern Mongolia, 1864-5; {{Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris (France) |id=P00721892 }} Sheet labelled ''Ulmus davidiana''; Armand David type specimen (2,) fruit and new leaves; eastern Mongolia, 1864-5</ref> The [[perfect flower|perfect]], wind-pollinated [[apetalous]] flowers are produced on second-year shoots in March,<ref>{{Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris (France) |id=P00721893 }} Sheet labelled ''Ulmus davidiana''; flowers and emerging leaves; Armand David specimen, eastern Mongolia, 1864-5</ref> followed by obovate [[Samara (fruit)|samarae]] < 19 mm (3/4 in) long × < 14 mm (1/2 in) wide.<ref>{{Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris (France) |id=P00721894 }} Sheet labelled ''Ulmus davidiana''; fruit and new leaves; Armand David specimen, eastern Mongolia, 1864-5</ref>
<gallery>

==Pests and diseases==
Evaluated with other Chinese elms at the [[Morton Arboretum]] in [[Illinois]], the tree was found to have a good resistance to [[Dutch elm disease]] (DED) <ref name=Morton>''Morton Arboretum Quarterly'' 31: 1-9, 1995</ref> [http://www.cirrusimage.com/tree_David_Elm.htm] [http://www.for.nau.edu/hbelm/elm_map.htm]. The species is reputed to have a good resistance to elm leaf beetle ''[[Xanthogaleruca luteola]]'', [[Elm yellows|elm yellows (elm phloem necrosis)]] and [[leafminer]]s in the US.<ref name="Morton"/> [http://www.for.nau.edu/hbelm/elm_map.htm]

==Cultivation==
The tree was briefly propagated and marketed by the Hillier & Sons nursery, [[Winchester, Hampshire]] from 1971 to 1977, during which time only four were sold.<ref name="Hillier,a">Hillier & Sons (1977). ''Catalogue of Trees & Shrubs''. Hillier, Ampfield, UK.</ref><ref name="Hillier,b">Hillier & Sons ''Sales inventory 1962 to 1977'' (unpublished).</ref>

There are no known [[cultivar]]s of this taxon, nor is it known to be in commerce beyond the United States.

===American testing===
The David Elm has shown some promise as a result of testing at the [[Ohio State University]] (OSU) in [[Ohio]].<ref name="Sydnor"/><ref name=Struve>Struve, D. K. and Rhodus, T. (1990). Turning copper into gold. ''Amer. Nurseryman'', 172: 114-123.</ref> At OSU, the plants were cultivated in copper-lined pots and planted in a wide lawn under a powerline and in small home lawns. The tree's performance has been mixed, but shows potential. Some specimens did extremely well, while others struggled. The tree seems to perform well on disturbed sites, in calciferous (alkaline) soils, and also seems to have a better tolerance for wet soil than the literature has indicated. A number of strong saplings were cultivated that show promise. Some saplings underwent judicious pruning early on to maximize structural stability of the plant ("pruning can help the plant result in a more structurally stable branching pattern" <ref name=Sydnor>D'Amato, N. & Sydnor, T. (2005). ''David Elm use for increasing biodiversity'', Columbus, Ohio, USA. [http://shade-trees.tripod.com/families/selections/david_elm.html]</ref>), and blue-colored tree shelters were used on some plants until the stem reached a diameter of 25–37 mm.

Additional observation shows that at least 50% of emerging leaves on the trees survived a hard freeze that lasted 5 days during April 2007. Leaves were approximately 70% emerged when temperatures fell to −6°[[Celsius|C]] (21°[[Fahrenheit|F]]). Temperatures fell below freezing for 5 days (April 4–8, 2007).

==Notable trees==
The UK [[Tree Register of the British Isles|TROBI]] Champion is a relatively young tree at White House Farm, [[Ivy Hatch]], Kent, measuring 5 m high by 17 cm [[diameter at breast height|d.b.h.]] in 2009.<ref name=Johnson>Johnson, O. (2011). ''Champion Trees of Britain & Ireland'', p. 168. Kew Publishing, Kew, London. {{ISBN|9781842464526}}.</ref>

==Etymology==
The tree is named for Father [[Armand David]], the French missionary and naturalist who introduced the tree to France in the 19th century.
